Editor's Column

APCS and the Psychodynamics of Academic Organizations

Mark Bracher

Mark Bracher

Mark Bracher  

APCS was founded on the proposition that psychoanalytic understanding can be used outside the clinical setting to benefit not only individuals but also groups—organized and unorganized, large and small. One way it can do so is by helping members of groups understand the psychological forces that gratify them and bind them together and those that, at times, frustrate them and drive them apart, as well as the psychological needs that push them to pursue and accomplish their collective tasks or, alternatively, to avoid or fail at their tasks. Given our assumption that psychoanalysis can help groups sustain themselves, accomplish their tasks, and provide gratification for their members, it is only logical that we attempt to make use of psychoanalytic understanding to improve the various organizations of which we are members—including academic organizations in general and APCS in particular. Thus in what follows, I want to sketch out some basic principles concerning the psychodynamics of organizations, identify a number of the more significant psychodynamic problems and resources that often characterize academic organizations, and, finally, explore some ways in which we might develop APCS to help it achieve its aims more fully.

We might begin by considering the general question: what are the characteristics of a successful organization, and what dispositions of psychological forces are most conducive to such success? By successful, I mean an organization that 1) has a significant mission and that 2) accomplishes this mission through mobilizing and directing the energies of the requisite numbers and types of people in a way that 3) produces a maximum of gratification and a minimum of suffering and frustration for these people and for those outside the organization.

Mission

For academic organizations—and since the great majority of APCS members are academicians, I will consider APCS to be, at present, at least, primarily an academic organization—the primary mission is threefold: 1) to produce new knowledge of a significant rather than trivial nature, 2) to disseminate this knowledge, both to other experts in the field and to students, and 3) to find new ways to put this knowledge to use to benefit people. Each of these missions faces significant obstacles that have psychological roots. The first mission is often compromised by activities that fail to produce any new knowledge at all—activities that simply rehearse old knowledge or repackage it—or by activities that produce new knowledge that is trivial rather than significant. Much literary criticism falls into one of these categories or the other. Even when literary criticism does offer previously unpublished interpretations, the human benefit of such interpretations is quite dubious, a point that most literary scholars recognize when they ask, “Does the world really need another article/book on ____?” Similarly, activities designed to fulfill the mission of transmitting new knowledge to others—activities such as teaching, publishing, and participating in professional conferences—often fail to achieve this end in adequate measure: many students acquire only a fraction of the knowledge that teachers are attempting to communicate, and scholarly articles and conference presentations are often received by a small audience and retained by only a fraction of that audience.

Marcia Ian

Marcia Ian

Marcia Ian   Associate Professor of Modern American and British Literature at Rutgers University, New Brunswick. One of the many ironies intrinsic to the Oedipus complex is that, although it stands for that structural principle that we know as patriarchy—i.e., the law of the father—the phrase “Oedipus complex” bears the name of the son, Oedipus, not that of the father Laius, whom he unwittingly killed and supplanted. The subjectivity analyzed and immortalized under the aegis of the Oedipus complex is not that of the father —who cares about him? he's dead—but that of the son, left to deal with his insufficient and apparently interminable guilt. While the phrase “le nom au père” designates the paternal anchor that holds down the symbolic order, it is actually le nom du fils, Oedipus, the son's name, which stands for the entire complex of associated psychosexual desires and drives, together with their familiar signifiers, including “le nom du père.”

The father is also notably absent from the social contract that constitutes his legacy, the genealogy of which is narrated, for example, in Totem and Taboo; this contract, according to Freud's narrative requires—is predicated upon—father's absence. The primary legacy of the Oedipal murder is a “group psychology” that forges solidarity through identification and collective guilt—not paternity, in other words, but fraternity (among the primal horde). It is still fraternity, another name for the “male bonding” of the omnipresent boys' club, rather than paternity, that is at the heart of many of our social ills, albeit a fraternity of men who usually end up being fathers too. (The checkered record of American men as fathers—the need to legislate against “deadbeat dads” or otherwise ensure that Father keeps his “promise” to the family—indicates a certain reluctance among American men to be fathers. And who can blame them?) America is run, not by a father or even a father figure, so much as a bureaucratized, corporatized network of interlocking, competitive fraternities—good ol' and not so good, not so ol', boys.

Father is not the point. The point is, how we feel about him, or rather how we feel about how we feel about him—a paternal effect, and affect, invented by, for, and about, us. We regularly accuse Dad of being absent too much, while we simultaneously complain that he is too much with us. Father is “absent” from the urban family where he has been made a scapegoat by many a psycho-social theory. He is absent from the suburban family where, as if this were still the 1950s, father is imaged by popular media as a tight-assed workaholic perennially at the office or hiding behind his newspaper or laptop. And he is absent even from modern German domiciles, according to Janine Chasseguet-Smirgel, who has blamed the Holocaust on too much German mothering. Most relevant to the present context, father is absent, except as the internalized threat of castration, even from the Oedipus Complex. The Oedipus complex is about Oedipus—about how his fate and his identity are engendered by the intersection, the interchangeability, of the father's desire with that of the son who replaces him. Poor Oedipus; he lost everything by becoming, in effect, the father who wished him dead.

Jeannie Ridings

Jeannie Ridings   Student in the PhD Program in the Human Sciences at The George Washington University.

If there is any one element that persists throughout the history of philosophy, it is perhaps the affirmation of philosophical inquiry itself. Although the ways in which thinkers have responded to particular inquiries differ, and there is inevitably confrontation between theoretical constructions, what unites philosophers qua philosophers is that commitment to inquiry—it is the central feature of our philosophical heritage. There is a certain eros inherent in ignorance, in our fundamental humanity, and in our desire to render our world comprehensible. Jonathan Lear explores what is at stake in our willingness to submit to inquiry, and the danger in positing that we already know the end of an inquiry.

Central to Lear's project is an analysis of the eros of inquiry—a passion clearly shared by the figures of his meditation, Freud, Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, and Wittgenstein. But Lear's take on the “eros of inquiry” is two-fold: he wishes, first, to defend Freud against contemporary critics, and second, to explore the resonance between early Greek thought and contemporary psychoanalytic inquiry. According to Lear, the desire to raise questions invariably turns back on itself and directs its attention to its own activity: the logos of the psyche. While it is easier to affirm the value of inquiry within the domain of philosophy, Lear responds to the specific critique of psychoanalytic inquiry. It would seem that as long as inquiry remains relegated to the more speculative realm of philosophy its vicissitudes are considered relatively benign. But psychoanalysis has received special attention in its interrogation of the human psyche, and its therapeutic claims.

Part of Lear's text is devoted to a defense of Freud's work and central insights. Contemporary critics find Freud an easy target, given that many of his claims were highly speculative and lacked empirical evidence. Further, the underpinnings of psychoanalysis remain entrenched in the idea of latent meaning, and a meaning specifically oriented toward the finesse of a therapeutic hermeneut.

Paul Roazen   Professor Emeritus at York University in Toronto, now lives in Cambridge, Massachusetts. He is most recently author of Canada's King: An Essay in Political Psychology. His other books include Freud: Political and Social Thought, Freud and His Followers, Erik H. Otto Rank remains one of the most talented, and least appreciated, among Freud's followers. Originally he came to Freud as a young student, and Freud encouraged him in every possible way; Rank became an intimate help-mate, and rewarded Freud's confidence by becoming prolific. It was Rank who was assigned the task of keeping the records of the proceedings of the group around Freud in Vienna, and therefore Rank's note taking became the basis for today's four-volume set of the Minutes of the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society. After serving as an editor of a military publication during World War I, Rank returned to Vienna and became a practicing analyst. Other of Freud's disciples were naturally jealous of Rank's unique status. A careful look at the famous 1922 group photograph of Freud and his so-called secret committee, selected to forward “the cause,” shows that Rank is the only one, standing immediately behind Freud's chair, whose eyes are looking in exactly the same direction as the master's.

After Freud fell ill of cancer of the jaw in 1923, Rank's rivals had their opening. Rank prepared himself to assume Freud's position, and then Freud rallied and went on to live until 1939. Freud's initial illness, however, became a decisive turning point in the relation between the two men. Freud was naturally none too pleased to read any newspaper articles about Rank's taking over as leader of the “movement.” Rank's little 1923 book on the birth trauma was intimately involved in his complex emotional relation to the founder of psychoanalysis. The text, full of original ideas and yet expressed loyally within Freud's framework, was dedicated to Freud, then thought to be in grave physical danger. Freud's initial reaction to the book was positive, but others in Freud's circle, such as Ernest Jones in London and Karl Abraham in Berlin, made things harder as they sniffed signs of psychoanalytic heresy in Rank's innovations. Freud always resented how Jones and Abraham had made things even more difficult for him with Rank. Rank travelled to America for lectures and supervision, and he and Freud attempted a series of reconciliations. Finally Rank moved to Paris in 1926, and a few years later quietly resigned form the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society. Rank had had one of the best theoretical heads among the early analysts, and he was able to develop his own independent ideas in a series of books. He never set up his own school, however, or acquired passionately devoted followers. His premature death in 1939, not long after Freud himself died, cut short Rank's career.

Richard Koenigsberg

Richard Koenigsberg   Director of the Library of Social Science, a marketing company that specializes in organizing and managing book exhibits for scholarly conferences. His books include Hitler's Ideology: A Study in Psychoanalytic Sociology (1975), The Psychoanalysis of Racism, Revolution and Nationalism (1977/1986), Symbiosis and Separation: Towards a Psychology of Culture (1989) and Hitler's Body and the Body Politic: The Psychosomatic Source of Culture (1996).

Psychoanalyzing Culture

To psychoanalyze society is to identify the unconscious sources of its cultural formations. For any ideology or institution we pose the question: “Why does it exist?” To understand an element of culture one seeks to uncover the psychic function it provides or performs. An ideology or institution comes into being and is embraced and perpetuated insofar as it does something (psychologically) for individuals within that society. Culture is a social construction. The question posed by psychoanalysis is that of the source of, or motivation underlying, the creation and perpetuation of specific cultural forms. For each ideology or institution we ask: What is its meaning, the psychological work it performs for members of that society?

Everything begins with the self. The fundamental illusion or resistance governing social and historical inquiry is the fantasy of the existence of a world “out there” separate from the human mind. What does “hegemony” mean? That some idea in the “external world” has been internalized to the extent that it controls our mind and body. Howard Stein posed the question: “Why can't we walk away from it?” Hegemony is the other side of the coin of attachment. The “dream of culture” (Stein) is the fantasy of “forces” outside the self that cannot be resisted, the existence of a realm of reality that is other than a human creation. We experience “society” as if it is hovering over us. The question is why we invest humanly constructed entities with such power.

Freud put forth the idea of “psychic determinism” as the fundamental principle permitting one to analyze dreams, slips of the tongue, and psychosomatic symptoms, proposing that there are no accidents in the life of the mind. Our unconscious mental life is the source of the images we dream at night, the mistakes and blunders of our everyday life, and the pains in our bodies. To psychoanalyze culture is to extend the principle of psychic determinism. We hypothesize that cultural formations and historical events do not happen by chance. There is a psychological source for what occurs in society, arising from the shared unconscious fantasies of its members. Culture is the externalization of our deepest unconscious fears and desires, providing the framework for expressing, articulating, and coming to terms with these fears and desires. To psychoanalyze society is to uncover the meaning and psychic function of specific elements of culture.

Adrian Johnston

Adrian Johnston   Currently a doctoral candidate in philosophy at SUNY Stony Brook. He is writing a dissertation that involves a revision of the metapsychological structure of drive in light of efforts to integrate a general theory of temporality into psychoanalysis. His recent and forthcoming publications include “Lacan's Purloined Linguistics” (Lacanian Ink 14), “The Object of Its Affection: Reconsidering Temporality and Object-Choice in Lacan's Theory of Sexual Difference” (The Letter), and “The Driving Force of Lack: Object a and Lacan's Extension of the Freudian Drive” (Psychoanalysis and Contemporary Thought).

Introduction

The Oedipus complex … is one of sublimation, which designates precisely an identificatory reshaping of the subject.

(Lacan, Ecrits 22)

You have, on one side, the theory of the Oedipus complex and, on the other side, you have the theory of metapsychology. On the one side we speak of Oedipus, the complex of Oedipus, the complex of castration. There we speak of the mother, the father and the child. We speak of the mother as primary object and the father as interdiction. There we speak of castration. On the other side, we speak of the psychic structure of function. We speak of thought, reality, pleasure. And those two parts remain fairly separate. What I saw … is that what Lacan has done—and we must realize what he has done is based very precisely on Freud—is to realize a unification of analytic theory which as such is the basis of psychoanalytic thinking.

(Miller 44-5)

The majority of criticisms leveled against the Freudian Oedipus complex derive both their strength and their often high degree of moral indignation from this complex's apparent grounding in historically contingent, gender-determined, and biologically tinged factors. Freud seems to be saying that a female mother and a male father are necessary presences for the generation of a properly human psychical organization. Such a simplistic conception of individual development, if Freud is truly being this straightforward, is obviously open to criticisms to the extent that the nuclear family is a relatively recent historical phenomenon specific to certain societies.

What's more, at this level of initial impressions, the mother is implicitly denigrated as smothering, anti-social, and the potential inculcator of psychosis. The father is raised to the position of being the agency of rationality, normalization, and socialization. Whether it's as a result of his own overall portrayal of this analytic concept or of the unfolding interpretive receptions and adaptations of it by his readers, Freud's version of the Oedipus complex as the universally necessary psychical “rite of passage” for human beings appears to rest on a whole series of tenuous, biased assumptions: inherent male chauvinism, loosely borrowed nineteenth-century biology and physiology, and hastily generalized anthropological contingencies.

Strip Culture

Michael Uebel

Michael Uebel

Michael Uebel   Assistant professor of English at the University of Kentucky, where he teaches medieval literature. The author owes his knowledge of psychoanalysis to Dakota, who turned him on to Reich. And if not for conversations with India, November, Renee, Asia, Chelsea, Sierra, Katrina, Becca, and Candy, theorizing strip culture would have been impossible.

Not long ago, I was in a low-end strip club in Washington, DC with an anthropologist friend of mine. It was there, in this club which still resembled the Chinese restaurant it had once been, that we started thinking about the operations of desire and the flows of power we saw condensed before our eyes. For we immediately grasped that the dynamics which we were participating in and observing were not only replays of the class- and gender-hierarchized culture just outside the red-curtained door, but that the dynamics here were in fact intensely magnified, to the point that, instead of becoming unbearable, they had become strangely tolerable, enticing even.

You see, we entered the club half-expecting a kind of utopic space to appear magically, offering us momentary reprieve from the operations of “surplus repression,” Marcuse's famous term for the unhappy regulation of sexuality under advanced capitalism. Well, we didn't—or couldn't—find any such relief; instead, the very liberation of sexuality the club promises, and no doubt partially delivers, actually produced in us states of submissiveness and acquiescence that we perversely found more satisfying.

There were questions now: How does a strip club activate, or reactivate, one's masochism? Where to look for the origin and nature of this pleasure in submissiveness? What are the contact points between a psychoanalysis of perversion and a cultural analysis of this erotic scene?

For sure, sexuality in a strip club seems less repressed. Sexual banter, unabashed naked bodies, the free exchange of money and compliments, and open seductions all seem to work at lifting prohibitions on sexuality. But, as Foucault reminds us, signs of sexuality's liberation point directly to the reaffirmation of the very structures that liberation and transgression would undo. If strip clubs are spaces for the possibility of a sexual existence unencumbered by sexual repression, they are so only to the extent that such an existence has been created or manipulated by an oppressive psychic and social order for its own purposes.

The Rebirth of Psychoanalysis in Russia

Gary Goldsmith

Gary Goldsmith

Gary Goldsmith   Co-Chairman of the Committee on Russian-American Educational Exchange of the American Psychoanalytic Association; Chairman of the “Russian and FSU Focus Group” of the International Psychoanalytic Association's New Groups Committee; Director of Russian Language Psychiatric Services, Beth Israel-Deaconess Medical Center in Boston; a faculty member of the Psychoanalytic Institute of New England, East (PINE); and Clinical Instructor in Psychiatry at Harvard Medical School. For the past four years, he has travelled to Russia three times a year to teach psychoanalysis and psychotherapy and to provide consultation for newly organized training groups.

The decade of the 1990s has witnessed an energetic revival of interest in psychoanalysis in Russia. Even prior to the breakup of the Soviet Union, the relaxation of restrictions under glasnost had permitted the republication of translations of Freud, with discussions about analytic theory—even treatment along psychodynamic lines—once again attracting attention. However, it is only in the last several years that formal programs of study among self-selected groups of Russian professionals, mostly in collaboration with western colleagues, have engaged the Russian mental health and academic communities. Interest in this movement lies first in the formal and longterm process of training new psychoanalysts and psychodynamically oriented therapists in a society where an educational structure, models for identification, and a culturally embedded psychoanalytic tradition were absent for three generations, and further, in the opportunity to observe how a society long hostile (in its official structures) to psychoanalysis confronts these changes. Although it is premature to draw conclusions regarding the public's reaction, the work of the practitioners themselves, their rhetoric, and their organizational efforts offer clues to the manner in which this by-product of democratic change is received and integrated. First, it is pertinent to provide a schematic review of the history of analysis in Russia.

Russian analysts were active in the spread of psychoanalysis in the early part of the century. For example, the first translation of Freud into a foreign language was the Russian edition of The Interpretation of Dreams in 1904. The contribution of Russian analysts is documented by the positive reception of the journal Psychotherapy, which began publication in 1910 under the leadership of Nikolai Osipov and Nikolai Vyrubov. It soon became the editorial nucleus of the field in Russia, publishing not only original Russian psychoanalytic studies and reviews, but works in translation as well. The fervent activity of Russian analysts in the 1910s was noted by Freud in a letter to Jung in 1912: “In Russia (Odessa) there seems to be a local epidemic of psychoanalysis” (306). Further comments followed in The History of the Psychoanalytic Movement (1914), where Freud wrote that while “a really penetrating comprehension of analytic theories” had not yet occurred, he could single out Moshe Wulff as an exception (33). (Wulff later went on to found the Israeli Psychoanalytic Association; Osipov became a founder of the psychoanalytic movement in Czechoslovakia.) In those years a significant portion (one eighth) of the entire membership of the International Psychoanalytic Association was Russian. Other active voices at that early time include those of Sabina Spielrein and Tatiana Rosenthal (whose study on Dostoyevsky influenced Freud's own paper “Dostoyevsky and Parricide”).

Lynne Layton's Who's that Girl? Who's that Boy? Clinical Practice Meets Postmodern Gender Theory offers an excellent example of combining and relating postmodern theories of identity and gender with relational theories of psychoanalysis. This work argues that a needed dialogue between postmodern theorists and psychoanalytic practitioners has not occurred because postmodern thinkers have tended to concentrate on abstract conceptions of social subjection and have thus ignored the ways that social constructions are internalized through meaningful relationships. Layton also points out that many object relations psychoanalysts have often neglected the ways that culture shapes all relationships and identity formations (11). In order to overcome this blockage of dialogue, Layton concentrates on the different and similar ways that these two approaches deal with the questions of subjectivity, agency, gender identity, narcissism, and development.

In her Introduction, she points out that postmodern and relational theorists often combine and confuse the definitions of the self, the individual, and the ego (12). She posits that postmodernists see all of these categories of agency as narcissistic constructs (12). In order to support this point, Layton turns to Lacan's theory of the mirror stage as a postmodern example of the equation between the formation of the narcissistic ego and the structure of the self and individual. She points out how Lacan and other postmodern thinkers connect this narcissistic self/individual/ego to a theory of social subjectivity grounded on the subject's need to encounter a loss of narcissism through the acceptance of social and linguistic castration: “A Lacanian clinician, then, as well as a Lacanian critic, figures the cure to the ego's narcissism to be the acceptance of the condition of lack” (13). This reading of Lacan's conception of analysis is centered on the movement from the narcissistic ego to the subject of linguistic castration and thus reinforces a dualistic interpretation of Lacan that avoids the essential concepts of the unconscious, the real, transference, and the object, a.

This book fits in a class with only a few books that are published in criminology/criminal justice each year—those that are non-textbooks and non-literature reviews and that are thought provoking. Not surprisingly, many of the books in this genre come from the same publisher, Garland Publishing, in its “Current Issues in Criminal Justice” series.

This book provides history, substance, and understanding to an issue that has been the topic of a great deal of debate in the past twenty or so years: legal issues of the mentally ill. Since the time in America when we began large-scale deinstitutionalization of the mentally ill, legal battles involving the mentally ill and their involvement of the criminal justice system have steadily increased.

Postmodern thought is, perhaps, the most appropriate method of dealing with this issue. Who gets classified as mentally ill, how those classifications change, how the criminal justice system (particularly the correctional system) deals with those that are classified as mentally ill (or those that the law argues should be classified as such) are best addressed by the deconstruction of and attention to communication, language, and symbols of postmodernism. As such, this book sets the stage for those who would take on this line of research, thinking, and action.

The primary focus of the book is a postmodern and semiotic critique of the areas of mental illness, civil commitment, and criminal insanity as it crosses between the fields of mental health and criminal justice. As stated in the book, Arrigo attempts to examine the “overlapping effects of clinicolegal discourse and multiple meanings (signs) contained in appellate case and statutory law affecting the mentally ill.” By examining the words, both spoken and inferred, in the law and in the treatment of the mentally ill, Arrigo describes in broad terms how people are labeled and then treated within the mental health field and the criminal justice system.

Chapter 1 is an introduction to postmodernism and its relevance in addressing the legal ramifications of what Arrigo at times calls “psychiatric consumers.” For a reader with a basic understanding of postmodern thought, this chapter provides an excellent link between the two. Arrigo addresses the role and purpose of postmodernism and brings the language of mental illness into this paradigm. He addresses the role of power in language and points out how the mentally ill are at a disadvantage in the processes of labeling and developing terms (both legal and social) that are not detrimental to them. Although Arrigo certainly provides a solid introduction to the link between postmodernism and mental illness, it is questionable whether a person with no understanding of postmodern thought could easily follow the postmodern discourse set out in this chapter.

The madness of Oedipus has become Western reason.

—J-J. Goux

Re: Oedipus

“Oedipus” is used in more ways than we can count; he (or it) is uncountable, as well as un-accountability productive. Oedipus, and it is quite unclear what this word refers to, is a multiply divided and repetitive enigma that prompts an incessant murmuring through as many voices as can be called upon to utter the name, a name that surely did not come from the mother or the father, but, perhaps, from outside the fold or from the other family. Oedipus is living and dead—and neither living nor dead—existing only along that boundary line at which language positions us, subjecting us to the constrained freedom of speaking subjects. Oedipus is the subject of his own, which means our own, discourse about our place in the world. And he is also subject to the discourse of many others, including his own forgotten history. As are we all.

Oedipus, to repeat, is uncountable. Technology, on the other hand, is what really counts for us. It makes things, including human things, count, by counting. It makes sure we are tagged and numbered by placing us in the data-base. It creates value by counting at ever faster rates of speed, by digitizing, accumulating, archiving. By buying and selling that about us that can fit on a disk and travel the wires, echo and ricochet from satellites orbiting our point of arrival and departure.

Already and a very long time ago, Oedipus sets the scene for technological surveillance. He accomplishes this, in part, by installing a self-surveillance and self-guidance system called rationality within both his own interior and, by becoming the police, within that of the polis. Oedipus moves, without at first recognizing it, from inside to outside the polis, back inside and then outside once again, cast into exile by his own word. Fleeing from the oracular voice of Apollo, who spoke enigmatically long before Oedipus saw the light of day, the man of ideas passes through the riddle of the half-woman, half-beast and enters into the enraged turbodrive of the rational, of the “one who will know.

On Anthropologists on Oedipus

David Spain

David Spain

David Spain   Professor of Anthropology at the University of Washington, where he has been a member of the faculty since 1968. He received his PhD from Northwestern University in 1969. In 1966-67 and 1975, he did ethnographic fieldwork in northeastern Nigeria among the Kanuri. He is a graduate (1986) of what was then known as the Seattle Institute for Psychoanalysis (but he does not have a clinical practice). He has co-authored and co-edited several books on Africa and on various topics in anthropological research. His published articles touch on a wide variety of topics in anthropology, most notably on debates about incest theory.

Anthropologists are contrarians. In this country, in this century, the type-case was Margaret Mead. Contrary to the generally accepted psychological wisdom of the day (the 1920s), Mead offered data which she saw as showing that Samoan adolescents were sexually very active but had no anxieties about this. Shortly thereafter, she found that Manus children were realistic young proto-scientists who, contrary to Piaget, did not think more primitively, even, than adult “savages.” In addition, she claimed that in at least three groups living in the Sepik River valley of what is today Papua New Guinea, sex (biological gender) was not related to temperament. In England, the best-known anthropological contrarian, Bronislaw Malinowski, expressed his most surprising views in Sex and Repression in Savage Society (1927), where “as every school-boy knows,” he argued that what he referred to as the “doctrine” of psychoanalysis was in error in suggesting—no, in insisting—that the Oedipus complex was universal (vii).

Over the past 75 years or so, anthropological rhetoric may have softened a bit, but contrarians continue to be the norm (pseudo-paradox intended). The three papers of this anthropological panel illustrate this quite nicely. Although the data are better than Mead's by far and the stances taken are less rigid than Malinowski's, the contrarian aims couldn't be clearer given the stated topic of the meeting: “Oedipus Today.” Two of the papers seek to address Oedipus today from as distant a yesterday as one can usefully imagine, while the third takes up Oedipus, not in its “default” (positive) setting, but in its negative form.

As I see it, these papers, individually and collectively, have all four of the features of anthropology at its best. First, they are comparative, and the range of cultures and cultural materials considered is great. Second, they take seriously cross-species data and, in so doing, demonstrate that anthropology is far more than cultural studies and that Stanford-like departmental splits are symptoms, not solutions. Third, they are comprehensive in that the aim is to discover (create) general patterns, historically contingent though they must inevitably be. Fourth, they are critical; the talk may be about distant pasts and places, but the aim is to learn what one must in order to be usefully critical of ourselves today.

By all appearances, symbolic authority has undergone a dramatic decline today. Not only do people no longer seem connected by a communal bond (underwritten by symbolic authority), but, look as we might, it is difficult to discern any clearly functioning representatives of patriarchal Law. The most likely candidate—the person often referred to as the “most powerful man in the world”—has come under attack precisely because of his failure to fit the bill. Rather than embodying a position of symbolic authority, President Clinton seems more, as Jonathan Lear has argued recently, a kind of pre-symbolic authority, a version of the father of the primal horde, not prohibiting jouissance but monopolizing it for himself.

Few people dispute that symbolic authority is in decline, though what you think of it depends in large part upon your politics. If you're on the Right, perhaps you lament the absence of fathers, good role models, heroes, and strong leaders. If you're on the Left, perhaps you celebrate what Ernesto Laclau and Chantai Mouffe call the “proliferation of struggles” and “new forms of social conflict” (1), which both indicate and further symbolic authority's decline. It is my contention, however, that this decline is only illusory, that while symbolic authority seems to have undergone a decline in its influence, its power over contemporary subjects has in fact multiplied. This power is evident in the near disappearance of radical political activity today. The absence of symbolic authority and the corresponding prohibition of jouissance should—or so it seems—open up possibilities for jouissance and possibilities for all kinds of radical political activity. In short, we should expect to see all sorts of challenges to the hegemony of late capitalism. That we don't see these challenges—or, that we don't see any that have been widely embraced—suggests that symbolic authority, the agency of prohibition, has not disappeared but has gone underground. And underground—because it is underground—it exerts its control more powerfully than ever.

Postmodern culture is dominated by a series of contradictions that undermine the ability of students to write in a clear and coherent manner. Through the analysis of a diverse range of television programs in my composition classes, I have found that there is a constant production of both liberal and conservative messages at the same time, and that this cultural production of contradiction is derived from the spread of global mass-mediated capitalism. As Daniel Bell has accurately described, capitalism has always relied on sending the dual messages of saving and consuming, conforming and innovating, of individualism and mass culture. What has changed in postmodern culture is that the tension between these opposing values has been lost, and now one encounters the constant production of contradictory messages.

This circulation of conflicting belief systems renders obsolete many of the past forms of political and critical analysis. One can no longer simply decode social and cultural texts in order to discover the ways that the dominant class controls the masses by getting them to buy into the very ideological systems that oppress them. Moreover, the conservative desire to locate a consistent liberal agenda in our cultural productions has also become out-dated. Both modes of ideological criticism fail because they neglect to see how postmodern culture lives and thrives by coming down squarely on both sides of every issue. By reading Seinfeld as a field of signs, I will show how this constant circulation of conflicting messages produces in its audience a state of cognitive ambivalence and political apathy. This analysis, in turn, will allow me to formulate strategies to empower students in composition classes by developing skills and strategies aimed to combat cultural and subjective ambivalence.

In her powerful article “Maternal Thinking,” Sara Ruddick, an influential feminist philosopher, defends the thesis that maternal thinking is dominated by three interests: preservation, growth, and acceptability of the child (215, 216, 217). Ruddick stresses that these three interests are often in conflict, and that a good mother thus cannot be a perfectionist. A good mother, so she continues, must accept that “unqualified success in realizing [all three] interests is an illusion” (216). The conflict between the basic goals that a mother strives for in her relation with her child is the “objective basis for… maternal humility” (216). Ruddick sees further difficulties and conflicts in each of the separate maternal interests with her child. Thus in her role of preserving, the mother must walk a fine line between protecting enough and not overprotecting or controlling (217). Given the many challenges and uncertainties emerging in the fragile life of children, the mother needs not only humility but resilient cheerfulness as well (217). In her role as promoter of the child's growth, the mother encounters the challenge that the child's actions are “irregular, unpredictable, often mysterious” (219). To deal successfully with this challenge, Ruddick claims that mothers adopt two philosophical attitudes. They are mentalists, not behaviorists, because they try to see in the changing behavior the continuity of one person. They are also personalista because they understand that listening to the child's fantasies gives them a better way to understand the meaning of the child's behavior than simply looking at his or her acts (219).

The third interest of a mother is making her child acceptable to other people. This involves the socialization task of the mother. Here too Ruddick sees that a profound tension is present. This time it is between what mothers want to make of their children and what the current “patriarchal” society expects from them (220). Ruddick's attitude toward this third tension is completely different from her attitude toward the tensions created by the two previous maternal interests. Whereas Ruddick argued that the first two tensions had to be accepted and that mothers created special attitudes to deal with these tensions, now she argues that the tensions emerging from the third maternal task must be dealt with by rejecting one pole of the tension—i.e., the demand that children be made acceptable to the patriarchal society. Such a demand has no legitimacy in her view, because in such societies there is “military and social violence and often… extreme poverty” (220), and because in such societies mothers “have been governed by men, and increasingly by managers of both sexes, whose policies mothers neither shape nor control” (220). As a result, argues Ruddick, a mother is asked to train “her daughters for powerlesness, her sons for war, and both for crippling work in dehumanizing factories, businesses, and professions” (221). A mother is also asked to train “both daughters and sons for defensive or arrogant power over others in sexual, economic, or political life” (221). Many mothers accept the tension between the often conflicting tasks of molding the child so that it becomes acceptable to the next generation or so that they themselves can be proud about it. About mothers who accept that tension, Ruddick writes that they live in an inauthenticity whose main attitude toward life is that of obedience as a consequence of “social powerlessness. [Their] maternal work is done according to the Law of the Symbolic Father and under His watchful Eye, as well as, typically, according to the desires, even whims of the father's house” (222). For Ruddick the real solution is for mothers to develop attention and love. About that attention and love she writes two things. First, that it is a special gift of women embodied in maternal thought.

I was surprised and curious when I heard of Anthony Elliott's new book on John Lennon. I know Elliott, the author of Subject to Ourselves (1996), Psychoanalytic Theory: An Introduction (1994) (reviewed in JPCS 1:2 [1996]), and Social Theory and Psychoanalysis in Transition (1992), as a psychoanalytic social theorist and commentator. He is now, I thought, doing psychobiography. Then I saw the title, The Mourning of John Lennon, and I expected cultural psychoanalysis—of us, not Lennon. Elliott's latest turns out to be both—the “mourning” is both Lennon's and our own—together with a bit of hagiography and some psychobiography of Lennon's biographers.

While hagiography has pejorative connotations, Elliott is convinced that after Albert Goldman's caricature in The Lives of John Lennon (1988) and Frederic Seaman's bitter The Last Days of John Lennon (1991), a sympathetic treatment is in order. Moreover, Elliott is aware of (indeed quotes) Freud's warning that biographers “fixated on their heroes,” tend to idealize and “smooth over” imperfections (qtd. 31-32), and Elliott even criticizes Ray Coleman's two-volume John Lennon (1985) for “cleaning up … the messiness of lived experience” (32). Coleman's account of the “heavy toll” taken on Lennon's first marriage by the stress of life with a pop star, and by drugs that “entered” that marriage “quite innocently” (qtd. 31), sounds like the audio-tape that visitors to Graceland hear in portable headsets (Elvis was “taken from us,” etc.). Even as Elliott works hard to avoid hagiography, he is a great fan of Lennon—Lennon's music, lyrics, social criticism, and death obviously influenced Elliott profoundly, and the more he researched his subject the more impressed he became.

For Elliott, Lennon was not only a stunningly original songwriter who “used his fame to advance the cause of world peace” (3); Lennon's life is a triumphant example of one who overcomes the pathologies of his own childhood and of celebrity to live life on his own terms and to create a phenomenal artistic and political legacy. Readers of Elliott's Psychoanalytic Theory: An Introduction (1994) know that of all the psychoanalytic theorists he surveys, he is especially enamored of Castoriadis' notion that the human imagination can be recovered within postmodern social institutions and conditions to permit subjects to create society anew. While Elliott never mentions Castoriadis in his “metabiography” (7) of Lennon, Lennon appears to epitomize for Elliott the creative subject in a new project of autonomy. Elliott thus discovers another “untold story” about Lennon by viewing his life as emancipatory—from the melancholy that followed the losses of his father (who left when John was two)

Elizabeth Cowie's useful and wide-ranging book Representing the Woman: Cinema and Psychoanalysis has three sizable objectives. Overall, the book sets out to respond to certain feminist calls for positive representations of women as a means of visualizing alternatives to patriarchal constructions of Woman. Second, the book reconsiders Freudian and Lacanian concepts such as identification, fantasy, fetishism, the drives, castration, and the gaze, in the interests of adding to the psychoanalytic understanding of gender formation and desire. Finally, in these contexts of representation and psychoanalysis, the book focuses on film in order to refine film theory's use of psychoanalysis to describe how narrative positions the spectator, how the spectator identifies with the image, and how cinematic representation operates in relation to desire.

A well-integrated collection of previously published and new material, dating from 1978 to the present, Representing the Woman grounds itself in feminist concerns over representation before moving on to the extended consideration of psychoanalysis in film studies.

Introduction: From Experience to the Real of an Experience

I have chosen to approach the topic “Theory & Experience” from the perspective of social change. I am interested in how theory relates to issues of intervention, whether legal, political, or cultural—interventions in the name of an Ideal which aim at some sort of change at the level of experience. More specifically, I am keen to investigate circumstances in which current strategies of intervention fail ox are at least problematic. I want to suggest that these anomalies, studied more closely from a psychoanalytic point of view, may provide a lever with which to revisit and rearticulate traditional approaches to intervention.

I want first to be clear about the kind of experiences I am interested in. We might think, for instance, of the experience of drinking a cup of coffee, of an argument with a colleague or parent, of striking a tennis ball, of being arrested, of smoking a cigarette, of going through a divorce, etc. We could even say that it is the totality of such experiences that shape, and are shaped by, our society, our institutions, and our identities—an idea that has almost reached the status of a cliché.

However, these background experiences that we recognize as shaping our institutions and theories are not exactly what I want to focus on. I am interested in the kind of experience that resists assimilation into conventional theoretical knowledge and understanding, what I will call the real of an experience. In this way I am establishing an opposition, at least for the purpose of this presentation—an opposition between experience on the one hand and the real of an experience on the other; or, to put it another way, between structured or symbolized experience on the one hand and, on the other hand, the kind of experience that remains enigmatic, even bothersome, insofar as it either persists in being ignored by standard world views or stubbornly insists on tripping up our theoretical attempts to grasp it. This, then, is a kind of metatheoretical observation that highlights what, from the perspective of conventional theories, are either Kuhnian anomalies or simple blind spots. So for the purposes of this presentation I am insisting on a distinction between, on the one hand, structured or meaningful experiences, experiences that are—and I take this for granted—discursively mediated, experiences that belong to the level of discourse, and on the other hand, experiences of the real, experiences that are not reducible to discourse.

The US Constitution differs from the Westminster system. Both have three distinct branches of Government: the Executive, the Legislative, and the Judicial. But in the US system the Executive (the President) is elected separately from the Legislature (the Congress), whereas under the Westminster system, the Executive (the Government led by the Prime Minister) is elected by a majority of the Legislature (the House of Commons). Thus it is possible in the US to have a President from one party and a Congress dominated by another party. This can produce power struggles between two of the arms of government, with the third, the judicial, being drawn in from time to time. This split does not occur under the Westminster system.

I think the US system developed as it did partly because King George III suffered from porphyria. Combined with natural adolescent emancipatory energies in the American colonies, the mad king and his unwise government (see Barbara Tuchman's book The March of Folly) succeeded in provoking the American colonists to fight for independence and construct a new constitution. In order to avoid the establishment of any such mad ruler under their new regime, they decided that not only should their “king” be elected and not hereditary, but also that a system of checks and balances should be able to control an elected president if he became mad (or bad) too. This led to the separation of the executive (The President) from the legislature (Congress).

It's as if there is a schizoid split at the heart of the American political system, which often works well (in terms of balance of power) but at times produces bizarre effects. The Clinton public humiliation by the Starr machine was one such effect.

I think a suitable metaphor for the US Constitution is the image of Iron John, as described by Robert Bly. Iron John is a wild, hairy, strong man, kept in a cage in the centre of the King's courtyard. The US created a President who is by far the most powerful man (or woman) in the world, yet is kept in check by the cage of Congress. The history of relations between the President and Congress describes the efforts of Iron John to escape the cage and act freely. This is followed by the efforts of Congress to recapture him and reassert control.

Upon reflecting on the relation between theory and experience it is impossible to miss a constitutive and paradoxical tension marking this whole domain. Since Lacan was so fond of paradoxes, a Lacanian approach to the theory/experience dyad seems pertinent and justified; moreover it might prove revealing. Let's start, then, with mapping the contours of this paradox or tension, a tension that is neither epiphenomenal nor accidental. On a fairly simple level the main purpose of theory seems to be to approach and account for experience and then direct our praxis, that is to say guide and “canalise” experience and action in ethically sound and “legitimate” chanells. This is a very simple and almost “neutral” statement. It is a widely shared belief that “the main reason for believing scientific theories is that they explain the coherence of our experience.” This is, in fact, a quotation from Alan Sokal's now infamous book (Sokal and Bricmont 55). The problem is, however, that theoretical inquiry and theory construction continuously fail to account for and understand the totality of experience, let alone to predict and direct human praxis. Even in Sokal's text, where the “holy” integrity of science is defended at all cost, the aforementioned statement is true only if we reduce experience to scientific experiments and scientific theories to the “best-verified ones”; this is again a quotation (Sokal and Bricmont 55). The problem here is, however, that scientific experiments constitute an already domesticated field of experience, a field of measurements that are already paradigm-determined—that is to say, contaminated by the same theory they are called to verify (Kuhn 126). Nevertheless, the verification they provide usually seems enough to sustain the fantasy “that the scientific community knows what the world is like,” the fantasy that “verified” theories adequately represent the field of raw experience (Kuhn 5).

It is this circularity of an already symbolized experience sustaining the fantasy of a closed Other of theory that reveals the nature of what Thomas Kuhn calls “normal science.” But the circularity of this play between theory and experience can be sustained only when something is excluded; what remains outside the equation is the unsymbolized part of experience, what always escapes symbolization and theoretical representation—in short, the real, the real of experience. Theory can only appear as a truthful representation or adequation of experience if the field of experience is reduced to that which is already symbolized, if the real is reduced to reality (which is constructed at the imaginary and the symbolic level). What is disputed here, then, is not that theory can be truthful to reality; it can. But this is a reality already produced through symbolization; it is a “theorized” reality. Theory can be truthful to the reality of our experience and still miss or repress the real of experience, what falls outside the grasp of this reality.

Introduction

This paper is in a study in the psychological linkage between individual, workplace (group), culture, and history. It explores organizational change as a “window” on catastrophic change in larger social units such as ethnic group or nation. It examines the (1) general cultural forces in the United States through (2) the psychodynamics of downsizing and managed care, which is explored via (3) the process of projective identification.

Substantively, then, this paper is a study in downsizing, managed care, and the potlatching of American society—that is, an attempt to understand cultural self-destructiveness. It builds on a longitudinal study of a hospital downsizing (Allcorn, Baum, Diamond, and Stein), and on an exploration of the language of euphemism in the corporate construction of reality (Stein, “Euphemism” and “Organizational Euphemism”) in the United States. It is an inquiry into the shared delusion of cultural normality, one created, enforced, and perpetuated by the dialectic of projective and introjective identification. It interprets economic explanation as obligatory mystification of brutality.

Methodologically, it inquires into how one “knows” culture psychodynamically. It emphasizes the role of countertransference as the central organizing principle of all human knowing. Its net ranges from anthropology and astronomy, to organizational psychology and consulting, to zoology. The knower is part of the knowing, part of what is known and what must remain unknown. The knower is the best and worst and ultimately only instrument of knowing (see La Barre).

I shall (1) explore how the general culture enacts projective identification (as is specifically manifest in downsizing and managed care), and (2) through two case examples, describe how culture analysts and critics can use their own countertransference to detect, understand, and intervene in often overwhelming interpellative forces. Downsizing and managed care will illustrate this process. With organizational data, I will attempt to show how projective identification “works” culturally, for both subject and target.

However important establishing a relationship with reality may be for the individual's survival, we should never underestimate the danger individuals perceive reality to pose for them. The danger to which I refer here is not the danger of this or that version of reality, but of reality itself, which is to say of a sphere of existence outside the individual's subjective control. Because of the threat reality poses, the individual's life project as often as not becomes that of dismissing reality rather than living creatively in relation to it.

Our ambivalence toward reality is nowhere better exemplified than in the idea that (social) reality is “socially constructed.” This idea attempts to deny social reality any claim to objectivity grounded in a relationship with natural imperatives, for example as their symbolic expression. At the same time, however, that social construction emphasizes the sui generis quality of social reality, it also calls into question those qualities that could make our social being real: that it is non-arbitrary, and that it endures. If it does not endure, in what sense is it real? Would it not be better, then, in thinking about the experience of the social world, to focus attention on its contingency and indeterminacy (Bhabha 171-2)?

A specific application of the idea that social reality is “constructed” is of special importance: its application to understanding the individual. To understand reality as a social construct means to understand the individual as a social construct, as a meeting point of socially produced identities. But, social construction has more significance than this. At the same time that it locates the individual in the intersection of social identities, it also suggests a project, which is to undermine the definition of the individual on the basis of identity. This project is supported by the judgment that identity is on the surface, and does not reach down to the depths of our being (Bhabha 48). Identity is on the surface because it is a product of the way we are seen by others.

Editor's Column

Psychoanalysis and Education

Mark Bracher

Mark Bracher

Mark Bracher  

In addition to being a prerequisite for much individual accomplishment and fulfillment, education is widely recognized as a key element in social change, functioning either as a vehicle for change or as an impediment to it. In many ways the most powerful of the ideological state apparatuses, education plays its dual role in social change in part by inculcating values, ideals, beliefs, and knowledge that work either to support or to undermine the status quo. In addition, by providing knowledge, skills, and other cognitive and emotional capacities to the disenfranchised, education functions as a primary means through which members of oppressed groups can become empowered. And finally, by developing in members of the empowered classes the cognitive and emotional capacities that are necessary for qualities such as empathy and vision, education nurtures the psychological roots of justice and humanitarianism. Those who wish to promote greater justice and reduce suffering thus often look to education to produce these ends.

Their hopes are often frustrated, however, because students frequently fail to learn what their teachers are trying to teach them. Usually their teachers attribute the students' failure to learn to lack of cognitive ability or intelligence, or lack of interest or motivation, and respond with redoubled efforts to instruct, interest, motivate, and/or inspire their students. Such assumptions on the part of educators are of course valid, as far as they go. But what they fail to recognize is that not only motivation but also interest and even cognitive ability have psychodynamic foundations, and that these psychodynamic foundations can be engaged in ways that can overcome many of the obstacles to learning. Psychoanalysis thus has much to offer education.

Psychodynamic Obstacles to Learning

Intrapsychic Conflicts Between Identity and Knowledge

In the first place, psychoanalysis can help us recognize and intervene in various kinds of psychodynamic obstacles to learning. The most obvious are the threats to identity that various aspects of education can pose. Such threats derive from what is known as the “subjective curriculum” (see Jones)—the specific, emotionladen meanings that a particular subject matter or topic can have for certain individuals or groups of students—and these threats can be embodied in any number of apparently innocuous bodies of knowledge. A student's ontological identity can be threatened, for example, by courses in astronomy that reveal the infinitesimal size of the earth in relation to the rest of the cosmos; by geology, archeology, or paleontology courses that demonstrate the temporal insignificance of the student's life in the context of geological time; or by anthropology, sociology, or history courses that provide knowledge of other, radically different values, beliefs, and governments. Similarly, students' sexual identity can be threatened by knowledge they may encounter in sociology, history, or literature classes that sexual practices their society or group considers perverse are normal in other societies or groups.

The origin of the family has been under discussion in modern paleoanthropology for several decades (see, e.g., Washburn and Lancaster; Lovejoy). This paper will suggest how the family became a critical adaptation for our ancestors at least one hundred thousand years ago. I define the family as consisting in a female, her offspring, and an adult male—who is of course the “father” to whom the title of this paper refers (see Brown 135, 136; Rodseth et al. 229). More specifically, the adults are sexual partners and they share goods and services. The female provides direct care for the dependent young. The male may also do this, or he may do so indirectly through caring for the mother.

Caveats

Many of the suggestions I will make can be challenged with plausible contrasting claims.2 But informed inferences must be ventured in studying human origins lest our understanding of these matters be immobilized by what David Nisbet calls sandheap empiricism. Most of my data will come from excellent studies, in the wild, of the chimpanzee by Goodall and of the bonobo by Kano. This is not to say that their findings apply with equal validity to all chimp and bonobo groups—and much is yet to be learned, especially about bonobos. But of the more recent work on these species I find these two studies to be the most thorough (see, e.g., Susman).3 For our purposes, such studies provide what might be called a “sideview” of human evolution which can supplement information derived from paleoanthropology, evolutionary psychology, psychoanalysis, and so forth. In general, I will hold that the family evolved in a shifting, disjunctive way, with innumerable false starts, hedged bets, failures, and small, sometimes isolated breakthroughs. Hence, I make two basic assumptions: that the family evolved gradually and that any brand of monocausality in identifying its origin and development is mistaken.

Running on Empty: Žižek's Concept of the Subject

Robert Resch

Robert Resch

Robert Resch   Teaches European Intellectual History at Texas A&M University. He is the author of Althusser and the Renewal of Marxist Social Theory and articles on postmodernism, Marxist social theory, Homi Bhabha, and George Orwell. He is currently working on a survey of Lacanian social theory.

In the following pages I argue that Slavoj Žižek's concept of the subject is ideological and that his arguments in support of it are obscurantist and incoherent. Far from developing a materialist Lacanian theory of the subject, as he claims, Žižek empties Lacan's theory of its material content and its scientific form in order to identify it with an existentialist notion of the subject as “empty” and with idealist notions of the subject as Cartesian cogito and Kantian self-consciousness.1 In the course of defending this conception of the subject Žižek willfully confuses distinctions between subjective and objective perspectives, between natural, social, and existential facts, and between epistemological and psychoanalytic categories. The result is not so much a theory as an Escher-like representation of a theory, a representation that is best understood by exposing the devices by which it deceives the reader into accepting the absurd as logical and the impossible as actual.

Toward A Realist Theory of the Lacanian Subject

In order to provide a background against which Žižek's errors will stand out clearly, it is necessary to outline a few basic principles and distinctions necessary for a coherent, realist theory of the Lacanian subject. Let us start with the notion of the human brain as the material embodiment of the Real, Imaginary, and Symbolic registers. We simply have to get used to the fact that memory, desire, drive, identification, and jouissance are all properties of high-level, interconnected neural networks acting in parallel within an astoundingly complex system that is the human subject.2 As schematized by Lacan's L- and R-Diagrams, the Lacanian subject is the simultaneous functioning of Real, Symbolic, and Imaginary registers—that is to say, the Lacanian subject is a totality (the RSI). Neither the Real, the Imaginary, nor the Symbolic subsystems taken individually can be thought of as a subject, even less as the “true” subject or as the “Lacanian subject.

Paul Verhaeghe

Paul Verhaeghe

Paul Verhaeghe   Professor of Clinical Psychology and Psychoanalysis at the State University of Ghent, Belgium. He is also a member of the European School for Psychoanalysis and the Association mondiale de la psychanalyse and author of Does the Woman Exist? (Rebus/The Other Press) and Love in a Time of Loneliness (forthcoming, Rebus/The Other Press).

According to Lacan, the sexual relationship does not exist: “Il n'y a pas de rapport sexuel.” In contrast to this rather depressing statement, let us start with the definition by Freud of a normal sexual life. In his Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality, we read, “a normal sexual life is only assured by an exact convergence of the affectionate current and the sexual current both being directed towards the sexual object and sexual aim. It is like the completion of a tunnel which has been driven through a hill from both directions” (Standard Edition VII 207). If we combine the two statements, the net result is that obviously the tunnel does not get completed and the two currents do not converge, so that the relationship doesn't succeed. As a matter of fact, usually one ends with two tunnels—that is, two relationships—one for the affectionate current and the other for the sexual one.

Moreover, as a further illustration of the problem, there seems to be a gender-specific divergence in the choice of chunnel. Women are said to have a preference for the affectionate one—that is, for love—while men are supposed to be more interested in sex an sich. As the saying goes, “In order to have sex, women need a reason, men only a place.”

My question for today is twofold. First of all, how can we understand this difference between men and women? And second, what are the consequences in terms of neurosis and perversion? As there appears to be a difference between Freud and Lacan in this respect, the answers could be quite important for clinical practice.

The major Freudian works of reference will of course be the Drei Abhandlungen, but also his Jenseits des Lustprinzips, and his last papers on femininity. The Three Essays are the starting-point. In the first essay, it is quite obvious that Freud is continuously using an implicit norm for the sexual relationship. He never gives an explicit definition of it, but we can deduce it rather easily, and it sounds very Masters-and-Johnson-like: a coital relationship between man and woman, resulting in mutual, although not necessarily simultaneous, orgasm and preferably in the missionary position. The irony, of course, is that the rest of the Three Essays gives ample evidence to undermine this whole idea, because the book concludes in the generality of the polymorphously perverse disposition of every human being. The most important concept in this respect is something Freud discovers in studying the sexual aberrations as well as infantile sexuality—i.e. the so-called Partialtrieb, translated in the Standard Edition as component instinct. I would prefer “partial drive”—drive because, once beyond the Anlehnung (anaclisis, in normal English: leaning to) to the vital somatic functions, it has nothing to do with instincts whatsoever; and partial because it concerns a component of a totality that is never there, that never reaches a conclusion.

Introduction

An internationally respected historian said, “Hostility and aggression in the political social world are created through murderous rage, persecutions and foulness, and the conscious and unconscious inner fantasies of the perpetrators. A moment's reflection will convince us that we are only able to postulate a characteristic or trait in another because it has been, to some degree, known to us in fantasy. Peoples and nations find in their minorities and in their neighbors an available and vulnerable target on whom to project their bad internal objects — their hatred and urge to kill, as well as their depreciated sense of inferiority, of being despised as slovenly parasites, cheats and unscrupulous characters. In the passion of nationalism, the enemy within becomes the enemy without” (Loewenberg).

The Nazi attempt at Jewish genocide was not just German. It was supported and encouraged everywhere the Germans went by other governments and the general population. Those “righteous Christians” (who saved Jews) were a small minority in the lands of Christian vicious anti-Semitism that fell right in with the destruction of the Jews. For nearly 2,000 years, Christians have been taught to hate the Jews and to treat them as the most hateful thing on earth: Christ Killers, Satan's Disciples, vermin, etc. The Holocaust could not have occurred without this basic Christian anti-Semitism. Such irrational hatred of others is an expression of self-hatred.

However, it is important to know that it didn't begin with the Nazis, that for generations upon generations the Jew in Germany and Austria and in much of Europe had been the object of denigration, depreciation to the point of being treated as less than human. Particularly during any time of stress, they became the object of abuse.

A Christian theologian, former Chairman of the Department of Theology at the University of British Columbia, said, “Is it possible that Christian humanism, the passion for truth, justice and human brotherhood, in which Christians rightly rejoice, and its compassion for sinners belong to the Jewish element transmitted through Jesus himself? Or has the power seeking, the cruelty, the support of and connivance and injustice and oppression, and above all the anti-Semitic and racial hatred that can, even today, successfully invoke the Christian name, represented pagan pollution of the pure stream?” (Nicholls).

Robert Paul

Robert Paul

Robert Paul   Candler Professor of Anthropology and Director of the Graduate Institute of Liberal Arts at Emory University, where he is also Coordinator of the Psychoanalytic Studies Program. A graduate analyst certified by the American Psychoanalytic Association, he serves as well on the faculty of the Emory University Psychoanalytic Institute and maintains a private practice in psychoanalysis.

In a series of publications, beginning with my ethnographic monograph The Tibetan Symbolic World (1982) and most recently in my book Moses and Civilization (1996), I have put forward the view that in our own civilization, as well as in a number of other social systems, political power and religion are linked not only to each other, but to a schematic narrative that, as I have argued and will show again presently, is Oedipal in nature. This narrative schema is remarkably consistent over centuries and indeed millenia, insofar as analysis reveals its presence behind Athenian tragedies no less than in the scenarios of such recent works as Star Wars, The Godfather, and The Lion King. The schema has a small set of very clear axioms and rules, but with it, it is possible to analyze, organize, and generate a vast array of narrative cultural productions from a wide range of places and eras.

I will not attempt, in this short compass, to give you a convincing reason why things are as I describe them; I will limit myself to describing how they appear to be. I begin with the observation that the matters I describe concern men, for the simple reason that in the relevant societies the public sphere and its associated domains of religion and political authority are predominantly if not exclusively male. Among the men, there are, it seems, two kinds, to whom I refer as senior men and junior men. Senior men are defined as having at least one of two perquisites that junior men do not: on the one hand, legitimate sexual rights to a woman or women, and on the other, recognized political power. Relative age is not as important as the presence or absence of these factors. I deliberately choose to say “senior men” and “junior men” rather than “fathers” and “sons” for two reasons: the former opposition is both more encompassing and more precise. The term “father” is, indeed, a very imprecise one, having a number of different components that may or may not appear together in one person: there is the biological genitor, the socially recognized pater, the one who nurtures and protects, and so on. Thus, for example, the question whether Laius or Polybus is Oedipus's “father” can only be decided by choosing either the genitor or the pater. The same is true of Moses's “father,” whose biological and social functions are split between two characters: Amram, an Israelite of the tribe of Levi, and an Egyptian Pharaoh, respectively.

Unconscious Dynamics of Oppression

Grant Schofield

Grant Schofield

Grant Schofield   Studied the sociology of religion at Cambridge and at Oxford, where he took an MA. He is the founder of Interface Ireland, an organization devoted to reconciliation. He is currently developing Communitas, a group that offers systemic workshops and with which he works as a Systemic Consultant in the border counties of Ireland and Northern Ireland.

At a Systems Workshop1 I participated in some time ago in Leitrim, Ireland, a context was created that was “not conducive to interpersonal interaction.” This was done through a seemingly chaotic placement of chairs such that it was difficult for any person in the room (including consultants) to establish eye contact with another. All participants were invited to engage with the task of the event, which was defined in terms of an aim and a process. The aim of the event was “To negotiate the ebb and flow of power,” and the process was “to provide opportunities for participants to risk interchange in the here and now about their ongoing experience of the event.” After an hour of tense silences interspersed with frustrated comments and expressions from participants, the consultants decided to offer a hypothesis. This they did in the form of an observation and a question. The director observed that one particular person had remained completely silent up to that point. He wondered if this had anything to do with the fact that a) this person was the only black person in the room, b) that she was the only representative from the third world among the membership, and c) that she was female. The reactions of participants to this intervention varied from anger, to surprise and shock, to defensive hostility. Demands were made that the person concerned speak up and give an account of her silence. Condescending insinuations were made that the individual did not have sufficient command of the English language, and therefore did not feel sufficiently comfortable (even in the face of evidence to the contrary from other events). Another reaction was to point out that this person was free to speak if she wanted to, that it was “none of my business that she doesn't want to speak.” The consultants responded to these reactions in three ways: a) by encouraging the person concerned to hold her silence, b) by asking for evidence in support of the allegations, and c) by asking for alternative explanations for the silence of this person. This resulted in a violent reaction against the consultants. Emotions were high, and various accusations were hurled. These included blaming the silence of this person on the layout of the chairs, accusing the consultants of “rude behavior,” accusing the consultants of running out of ideas and having to invent a hypothesis to save face, and attacking the aim and process of the event as obscure and totally meaningless.

Orphans, foundlings, children in need of substitute parents are an ineluctable piece of human history. The causes and effects of their parentless status have captivated the imagination for untold generations. Even a brief consideration of mythology, fairy tales, and literature, especially for and about children, underscores the power of the parentless child to stir both conscious and unconscious fantasy; attempts to understand the meaning and importance of these fantasies have occupied a pivotal place in psychoanalytic theories. Mythical children are raised by substitute parents for various reasons. Sometimes, as in the case of Oliver Twist or Little Orphan Annie, it is as simple as the death of the biological parents. In stories such as The Secret Garden, a child may be emotionally abandoned because he or she is held responsible for the death or disappearance of a beloved parent. At the other end of the spectrum is abandonment in an attempt to protect the child's life, as in the case of Moses, who is put into an ark of bulrushes to save him from the Egyptians, or Superman, who is sent away from Krypton before the planet is destroyed (see Widzer). In other cases, the absence of the biological parents is not explained. For example, we don't know why Dorothy lives with Auntie Em and Uncle Henry, or why Joyce's nameless child in the first three stories of Dubliners lives with his aunt and uncle, or how Huey, Dewey, and Louie come to live with their Uncle Donald.

In these stories the quality of substitute caretakers is as varied as the reasons for children's needing them. Some children are left with kindly, other-worldly creatures as are Romulus and Remus and Kipling's Mowgli, both cared for by wolves, or Sleeping Beauty, alias Briar Rose, who spends the first sixteen years of her life in the care of fairies disguised as simple peasants. Other children, such as Cinderella, may acquire an unsympathetic or wicked step-parent and fare less well. The fate of children raised by substitute parents varies as well. Some, like Oedipus, psychoanalysis's most famous adoptee, inadvertently or unconsciously destroy the parent who abandoned them, while in other cases, such as that of Luke Skywalker and Darth Vader, the destruction of the parent is more consciously determined. Others search until they are happily reunited with the lost parent of infancy. And some, like King Arthur, grow to bring honor to themselves and those who cared for them.
