Freud was sure that the Oedipus complex was his most important discovery; the basis of love and sexuality as well as the core of perversion and neurosis, it even seemed to figure in human origins and the hidden meanings of culture. Needless to say, Freud's assessment is not widely accepted. Many scholars question the very existence of the Oedipus complex, not to mention its usefulness for understanding personality and culture. Sociobiologists opine that animals, human beings included, have built-in mechanisms for avoiding close inbreeding. In the Westermarck version of this argument, inbreeding avoidance is activated by social familiarity. Whether the biological mechanisms alone or the mechanisms in combination with attachment produce incest avoidance, oedipality1 is unlikely or impossible (see Wolf). Discourse theorists often object in particular to the implication that the Oedipus complex lays the basis for romantic love and marriage. To their way of thinking, romance and marriage are social inventions, not the likely outcomes of normal childhoods (Katz). They contend that oedipality is irrelevant in any event in a world in which sexuality is increasingly shaped by street culture and the hyper-real imagery of the mass media (Simon). Psychoanalysis itself has been turning away from oedipality and sexuality for some time. Many psychoanalysts now doubt that oedipality plays a significant role in child development and focus instead on object relations.2

I argue nonetheless that there are good reasons for thinking that oedipality is everywhere important in the emotional development of children, male and female. It varies in onset, intensity, and duration, and it is subject to diverse idiosyncratic and cultural displacements in the symbolic register, but it is not peculiar to any one culture or type of family. It is no less important in contemporary society than in other societies. If anything, it is more so. Freud's critics and the post-Freudian revisionists miss the forest for the trees. Object relations—or what I prefer to call attachment—and social discourse are parts of the story but they are not the whole story, either separately or together. The forest comes into view when we put oedipality and language in evolutionary perspective, and when, with this perspective in mind, we consider how oedipality and its accession to the symbolic community vary with the quality of early attachment.

At the university where I teach there are not one but two institutes for the study of leadership, and the training of young leaders. When I asked one of my students why he was taking so many courses in leadership, he said it is because he did not want to be a follower. Are these really the only choices? Is it possible that the more we study leadership, the less we know about it? More likely it is a question of how we study leadership, and what we hope to learn.

I am going to make a simple argument about leadership. Most of the attributes that people associate with leadership, such as possessing a vision of the future, inspiring followers, and motivating laggards, gain their significance only within the framework of interpretation. Good leadership is interpretive leadership, a point that is frequently ignored, as we lack the categories to appreciate it. These categories look more like what Winnicott called holding and interpretation than they do grand strategizing and master-planning.

Good leadership interprets the hopes and fears of followers to them, so that they will not despair, or be overcome with anxiety. Winston Churchill's greatness, according to Franz Neumann (406-407), stemmed from his ability to transform an unknown danger “into a danger known in kind and extent. He fulfilled those functions of leadership that can be compared to those fulfilled in the life of the individual by the organization of the ego.” I will not be using the language of ego psychology, as Neumann does, but my conclusion is similar. Leadership is about interpreting anxiety, above all what Melanie Klein (“Mourning”) calls depressive anxiety: the fear that one is not good enough, mature enough, strong enough, and self-controlled enough to make good on the badness in the world, badness to which one has contributed by malevolence or neglect. Good leadership is about helping followers to face this anxiety, and thus put together the parts of themselves they keep separate so as not to know what they fear to know, their own weakness, immaturity, and incompetence.

Sheila Kunkle PHD

Sheila Kunkle

Sheila Kunkle   Assistant Professor of Social Sciences at Vermont College of Norwich University. Jacques Lacan refers to the Holocaust as a time when people acted as if they were under the power of some monstrous spell, when they sacrificed themselves to kill and torture for an Other who commanded tasks of extermination and loyalty (Four 275). While in the hold of this monstrous spell, the very ontology of the subject's universe seemed to alter, as limits of time, being, and motion changed and he entered an in-between existence, where life and death became fused.1 It is during such episodes that the subject is transformed into an uncanny replicant of his former self, and is compelled to commit acts that later will seem strange and inexplicable to him. From the collective acts of mass killing in genocide to the torturer's cutting of flesh and breaking of bones in political prisons, the perpetrator acts, often savagely, in a repetitive and deadly manner so as to experience the only kind of pleasure possible when the crucial space between reality and the Real closes: the pleasurable pain of an excessive and ugly jouissance.

Slavoj Žižek discusses this “ugly jouissance” in his analysis of Schelling's philosophy, which posits “the ugly” in topological terms, as that which is larger than its representation, an object out of joint, in the wrong place (Abyss 21-29). In this essay, I discuss what happens when subjects leave the world of meaning and subjectivity as we know it and enter the uncanny dimension of the Real, where “the ugly,” becomes “the lack that also functions as an excess, the excess of a ghostly, spectral materiality in search of a ‘proper,’ ‘real’ body” (Abyss 23). It is a place where das Ding, the Thing, makes its appearance, which “opens up the totality of our drives and all of the transgressive impulses in us” (Jaanus 4). It is the Thing, which is “the cause of the most fundamental human passion” (Lacan, Ethics 97), and “for which we will kill, suffer, die, work and sweat” (Jaanus 7). The Thing, in the words of Maire Jaanus, is not something we can objectively or directly prove, it is rather and paradoxically “our deepest interiority, something we can never eliminate, and yet, it is not us because we evolve beyond it a subjectivity with the other, the neighbor, and with the symbolic” (4).2 When ugly jouissance arises in the presence of the Thing, attempts at sublimation fail and the desublimation of the neighbor may occur, as happened in the 1994 Rwandan genocide, when ethnic Hutus at all levels of the society tortured, raped, and hacked to death over 800,000 of their Tutsi neighbors.3 Such atrocities transform bodies (the Imaginary) either into tools that work in the service of an ugly jouissance (the perpetrators), or into apparitional encasements of das Ding (the victims). Perpetrators acting in the Real are in part attempting to find their ontological coordinates and deal with the lack, which is also the excess—the unbearable kernel of jouissance, now located in the body of the other.

Introduction

Contemporary research on general homicide has shown that parricide rates are not affected by general rates of violent crime or the social structural variables (see Gilles; Green; Millaud, Auclair, and Meunier; Sadoff; Weisman and Sharma; but see Marleau and Webanck). The lack of variance in parricide rates across different periods suggests that traditional variables such as race and class are not causal factors in this crime. This fact, together with the stable rate of occurrence in both the United States and abroad suggests that the key causes of parricide are psychoanalytic, a factor that mainstream criminological research has often overlooked.

Parricide is similar to other “typical” homicide situations in that it resists boundaries of conventional definition: categorial identities such as “offender” and “victim” become murky. As homicidologists Richard and Carolyn Block state in their article “Homicide Syndromes and Vulnerability,” “the loser of the confrontation is the person who dies; the winner becomes the offender”(85). Thus researching homicide takes into consideration that the homicide event is the culminating point for a preceding series of actions by both participants. The event is deemed a “culmination” because that is where the interaction stops. Viewed in this light, fixed binary distinctions such as killer/victim are of questionable validity. The participants in the homicide event are dynamic, since the roles of the participants have shifted back and forth. In homicides, it is chance and/or (un)luck that stamps the final identity—through criminal law.

The sociologist Jack Katz understands homicides as assertions of morality and sensuous emotions. Put differently, those who kill do so to defend their version of the “universal good.” Thus when a husband “discovers” his wife with a mutual friend, the murder is an upholding of the killer's identity as a “good husband.” Or in robbery-homicides, when killers shoot innocent bystander-victims in cold blood, homicide is the “badass'” assertion of his identity as a transcendental being. Put in Lacanian terms, the versions of “eternal” and “universal” institutions of good can be understood as master signifiers (see Bracher).

The topic “Oedipus Today” develops an ambiguous representation. An initial interpretation seems to me to be based on the following prepositional sequence: for psychoanalysis, the “paternal function” is the psychic mainspring of the “law” that assures the establishment of the subject. The historical evolution of modern societies is unquestionably characterized by a decrease in the social power accorded to fathers. The decline in the social power of fathers therefore raises the question as to how, in the future, the paternal function, and thereby the constitution of the subject, can take effect.

In one form or another, this outline appears in the vast majority of works by “shrinks” (psychoanalysts, psychologists, psychiatrists) as well as by sociologists, historians, legal scholars, and social workers. This relative consensus among the historical and the mental-health disciplines has replaced the debates—now relegated to the past—about the universality of the Oedipus complex as formulated by psychoanalysts. Those who entered into discussion with the psychoanalysts at that time were primarily cultural or structural anthropologists. And the debate was mostly a theoretical one, focused on the applicability of the oedipal schema across a range of cultures.

Today, however, the discussions are more likely to engage the interest of historians, sociologists of the family, and jurists. And the latter are very concretely involved in the transformations of present-day societies. The importance of this shift in the framing of the problem may not have been given enough consideration.

Needless to say, the threefold schema that I have isolated here contains two insurmountable difficulties. The first of these difficulties is of a historical nature. No sociological work can rest content with time-worn considerations of “decline” (of the family, the father, and so on) without depriving itself, from the outset, of the means by which to think about its object—namely, the current forms of the family and the trends in their development. In other words, the ordinary account of “the decline of paternal power” implicitly conveys a nostalgia for the way things used to be, which, oddly enough, is always held to be better than the way they are now. Far from confining itself to the factual description of changes in family law, this account entails a large-scale evasion of the conditions that have transformed the modern family, conditions that cannot be reduced to a “decline.” In other words, fathers are no longer entitled to deny filiation. It is now clear that the Power of fathers, which is today reduced, was for the most part the power not to appoint a line of filiation.

Some years ago, I heard a colleague who was giving a paper make a joking aside about the unforeseen consequences of preserving confidentiality in case presentations. I'm not sure whether this is an old shrink's tale or it really happened, but the story he told was about someone who had published a paper about a client with asthma problems and a host of other psychological issues. Some enterprising behavioral medicine psychologist/researcher read the paper and thought he recognized important correlations between the psychic issues the patient had and the condition of asthma. So he began a research project that attempted to replicate these correlations, but the research project ended with no significant results. The researcher wrote to the person who had published the paper and found out, to his dismay, that the therapist had been trying to disguise his patient to preserve confidentiality, and one way he did so was to substitute asthma for what was really a gastrointestinal problem. At the time, I, and the rest of the audience, thought this was hilariously funny. But now, several years later, and two or three published case studies later, I don't find it funny at all. Indeed, I am rather paralyzed at the moment with regard to the ethics and conventions of both publishing case studies and of using them for instruction.

The case study is both one of the discipline's primary research tools and one of its primary teaching tools. It presents enormous learning possibilities but also raises a lot of ethical concerns. One of the things that makes therapy work is the assumption between patient and therapist of strict confidentiality. Thus, when writing a case study, particularly one in which treatment is ongoing, we must take great care to disguise our patients' identities. But as we know from the cases of Anna O., Dora, the Wolf man, etc., the disguises have never been good enough to keep the subject from being unmasked. In my own experience, it has been clear that any relative or friend of someone about whom I have written could easily recognize the person, especially if this intimate knows that the person was in treatment with me. So, the first layer of my paralysis has had to do with my sense that it really isn't possible to guarantee confidentiality. One way I have dealt with the problem has been to ask permission of my patient and have the patient read the piece.

I would like to discuss what is commonly known as Attention Deficit Syndrome (Attention Deficit Disorder according to the DSM-IV) in psychoanalytic terms. To date, the response as to how to treat this disorder has came mainly from the biological sciences, which propose diverse hypotheses regarding chemical unbalance in the brain to explain it. The quasi-universal use of Ritalin is also part of the medical response. Other trends in the therapeutic field, more promising in our view, emphasize that a connection between biology and the environment is necessary to produce attention deficits. Stanley Greenspan (1997) and his collaborators maintain that this disorder—as well as many other types of functional disorders in early childhood ranging from behavioral and learning difficulties to thinking disorders—should be considered the result of the interaction between the inherited genetic traits of a child, and how his/her environment—i.e., parents or caregivers—respond to that particular biological configuration. Among those who think that intelligence is more that simply the capacity to pass a test or perform mathematics, he maintains that in the origins of intelligence, the emotional exchanges between the baby and the caregivers are crucial to mobilize brain pathways and early behaviors that result on the development of cognitive and social capacities. His perspectives on childhood development and childhood pathology, arising from a wealth of clinical experience, are interest and insightful, and they deserve closer examination. I shall refer to them later.

More and more, especially in industrialized societies, the medical domain is taking the lead in responding to the suffering of the subject. An increasing number of symptoms (depression, anxiety, phobias, enuresis, asthma, etc.) are being displaced from any psychic consideration and relocated in the supposedly more scientific domain: the brain, the genes, and the neurotransmitters are now the efficient causes explaining why we feel sad or depressed or have addictions.

The Lacanian Clinical Field is a series designed with a twofold aim: to introduce Lacanian psychoanalysis as it is practiced in the clinic to the American psychotherapeutic community, and to bring the insights of the clinic to bear on the more academic uses of Lacanian theory. Juan-David Nasio's contribution to the series, Hysteria from Freud to Lacan: The Splendid Child of Psychoanalysis, translated by Susan Fairfield, presents a thorough, readable account of the paradigmatic neurosis of psychoanalysis—hysteria. Not only does he give a view of hysteria from today's couch, outlining its symptoms, causes, and possible cure, but he also provides an encapsulated history of the subject by tracing the phenomenon of hysterical blindness as it has been understood from Charcot to Lacan. Along the way, he delicately introduces the non-clinician to the processes undergone by the analyst on the path to understanding and helping analysands to “pass through the ordeal of anxiety” and accept and mourn the loss of the fiction that had heretofore defined their hystericized relations with the others in their world.

Daniel Buccino   Intern coordinator in The Community Psychiatry Program at The Johns Hopkins Bayview Medical Center and maintains a private practice in Baltimore. There is surely cause to celebrate Judith Gurewich's enthusiasm and The Other Press's publishing commitment to enriching the English-speaking psychoanalytic culture in their launch of The Lacanian Clinical Field Series, the first four titles of which are under review here. Though none of the four titles are breathtaking in their own rights, as a whole they constitute an essential addition to any psychoanalytic library, especially those engaged with Lacan and most especially for clinicians. The first four volumes in the series here represent the promise of establishing a more thoroughly Lacanian culture in the United States in the ready availability of many notable psychoanalytic works heretofore unavailable in English. Even in the variable range of quality of these initial offerings we see an opportunity not to highlight inadequacies, but rather an almost clinical opportunity to investigate further another neighborhood in the Lacanian village and reflect yet some more on the relationship of Lacanian analysis to larger psychoanalytic communities and other traditions. And having an opportunity to engage with the good, the bad, and the mediocre, the exceptional and the merely serviceable, the most doctrinaire and the more heretical, we can only expand the number of voices at play in the psychoanalytic village green, as it were, and we are afforded the chance to work with and work through positions that seem different, difficult, simple, or wrong.

It is in this multiplicity of voices, the repetitiveness of some of the information (especially in the more introductory and not specifically clinical texts), that Lacan will become more and more familiar in the United States. It is in this call to work, to converse, that psychoanalysts from various factional camps may come together to protect, preserve, and even advance the Freudian discovery, on the eve of the Library of Congress's belated opening of its purportedly epochal Freud show, at the end of the Freudian century, in the face of the marauding hordes who seek, quite simply, to destroy all that is psychoanalytic.

Racism, Hatred, and Discrimination through the Lens of Projective Identification

John Bird and Simon Clarke

Simon Clarke

Simon Clarke   Visiting lecturer at the University of West of England, where he teaches sociology and social psychology. His research interests include racism, the sociology of hatred, and psychoanalytic and sociological theory. He is currently researching racism and exclusion in higher education.

The Kleinian mechanism of projective identification can provide us with a more detailed understanding of how racism, hatred, and discrimination work. Traditional sociological explanation has failed to address some of the central issues surrounding racism: first, the ubiquity of forms of discrimination and the affective component of hatred; second, the rapidity, as in the case of the former Yugoslavia, with which communities that used to coexist can come to hate and destroy each other; and third, the embodied and visceral content of much of this discrimination. And finally, traditional explanation ignores any psychological structuring of discrimination; in other words, explanation is sought in social structures rather than in psychological mechanisms that may provide the impetus for people to hate each other. We believe that there is a complex interrelationship between socio-structural and psychological factors. Both need to be addressed in parallel if we are to understand the ubiquity of racism.

Our discussion has two parts. The first part explores mechanisms identified by psychoanalysts—in particular, projective identification—which, we argue can provide us with a more useful account of discrimination and hatred. The second part looks at the work of Frantz Fanon and Slavoj Zizek through the lens of projective identification.

Klein argues that in the paranoid schizoid position there is a splitting of good and bad objects, with the good being introjected and the bad being externalized and projected out into someone or something else. In the depressive position, good and bad are no longer split, difference is reconciled, and the individual attempts to make good, to make reparation for the damage that has been done or has been phantasied to have been done. These notions have been developed by Kleinians such as Bion in the context of individual and group psychoanalysis, but have rarely been applied to racism, hatred, and discrimination. We are particularly interested in one the earliest mechanisms of the paranoid schizoid position, projective identification, and the implication it has for the way in which we think of others, feel about others, and most importantly in terms of the structure of discrimination, how we make others feel. Projective identification is, for Klein, the prototype of all aggressive object relations and a crucial mechanism of defence. Projection per se is a relatively straightforward process in which we attribute our own affective state to others—in other words, we project onto rather than into. Projective identification involves a deep split, a ridding of unpalatable parts of the self into some other, forcing them to feel the way we do, or feel how we feel about them.

The Male Negative Oedipus Complex in Cross-Cultural Perspective

Robert Paul

Robert Paul

Robert Paul   Candler Professor of Anthropology and Director of the Graduate Institute of Liberal Arts at Emory University, where he is also Coordinator of the Psychoanalytic Studies Program. A graduate analyst certified by the American Psychoanalytic Association, he serves as well on the faculty of the Emory University Psychoanalytic Institute and maintains a private practice in psychoanalysis.

The Oedipus complex is a family drama, involving the key players in domestic society—that is, parents and children. But there is always more to society than the family or domestic unit. A distinctive feature of the vast majority of human social systems is the integration of domestic units characterized by some degree of legitimized pair-bonding and child-rearing into a wider network of relations that, while often framed in terms of an ideology of descent and kinship, is different from a family, and includes several such units in some sort of enduring, overarching relationship with each other. This encompassing system—roughly speaking the “public realm” as opposed to the “domestic” realm—operates on different principles, evokes different kinds of affects and behaviors, and may be understood both to incorporate and utilize, but also to attempt to negate or counter, the kinds of intimate family relations that prevail in the domestic unit. The mother-child relationship that necessarily forms the central social bond of the domestic unit is replaced by other forms of association in the wider sphere, and may indeed become an object of shame, secrecy, marginalization, or contempt in the public arena.

Life begins for each person in the domestic unit alone, and entails a more or less gradual or sudden separation from it and immersion in the wider arena of the public world. The family, as the initial scene of socialization, has the task of simultaneously creating primordial social and psychological structures in the child, while also providing for its own transcendence in favor of the encompassing relations that prevail outside it. In some respects, while the family shapes the conscious and unconscious life of the child irrevocably, it must also remain transparent to the cultural discourses and social values characterizing the wider world. To what extent, in any particular case, that outside world is a version of the family writ large, or, on the contrary, is constituted on new and even radically different structural principles, is an empirical ethnographic question that needs to be studied comparatively.

Introduction

A psychological study of Judaism and Christianity inevitably confronts deep-seated biases and prejudices. A dual focus on the psychology of religion and of ethnic identity is required, each of which invites misunderstanding and criticism. Those who feel, rightly or wrongly, that their religious beliefs are challenged or their ethnic identifications criticized may feel offended. Any effort to deny or to minimize the differences, however, inevitably must interfere with the objective investigation of the differences and their psychological implications.

Religion is a universal practice found in every known culture throughout history. There is a grandiosity in Judaeo-Christian religious experience expressed by the belief that we are created in the image of God, a belief accompanied by the reassuring assertion that physical death is not the end of our existence. Devoutly religious groups, however, frequently have not hesitated to persecute, and often to kill those whose beliefs differed from their own. Theists have struggled valiantly to rationalize the contradictions of a perfect God of Peace and the destructiveness and violence of human experience. Historically, there may have been many more persons killed in the name of God than persons saved as a result of efforts made in His name. Gautama Buddha's advice might be a cornerstone of human tolerance that has yet to be achieved: that we should respect the religious convictions of those who believe differently, because, for all we know, they may be right! History reveals the extent to which that advice has been rejected, especially by Christians in their relationships with the Jews.

The persecution of Jews throughout history was, and to a significant extent, continues to be rationalized by accusations of undesirable psychological and ethnic characteristics. These are obvious distortions based on the psychopathology and politics of anti-Semitic prejudice. Reaction-formations against such prejudice have also evolved, with idealization of the “Jewish intellect,” thereby contributing an additional source of prejudice based on envy. A simple rejection of such prejudicial attitudes is not sufficient, since significant differences between Judaism and Christianity do exist which profoundly influence the character and behavior of the members of each group, and which continually threaten to revive the fires of hatred on both sides.1

Between the Real of History and Historical Discourse: Philosophy of History as a Fantasy Construction

The reflections that follow concern the terrain of the philosophy of history, meaning the terrain of systematic interpretation of past events in accordance with a principle by which they become unified and acquire a certain meaning (Lowith 1). The past is irretrievably lost, and history can only make sense, can only be constituted as a meaningful discourse, by introducing into a series of floating traces (that as such have no fixed meaning) “some transcendent purpose beyond the actual facts” (Lowith 5). This was already pointed out by Hegel in the Philosophy of History: The spirit of the historian is quite other than that of the times that he treats but the historian, as a “workman,” can only approach “his task with his own spirit; a spirit distinct from that of the element he is to manipulate” (Hegel 4-5). For Hegel even the “original historians” (meaning Thucydides, Herodotus, etc.) had to organise their material in such a way—like poets. The only difference was that since they had limited their interest within their own times, their own spirit was not different from that of these times in general. History thought without the introduction of this organising spirit, without Lowith's transcendent purpose, can only be “a vast picture of changes and transactions; of infinitely manifold forms of peoples, states, individuals, in unresting succession” (Hegel 72). This anarchical meaningless ensemble can only acquire meaning through its articulation in a meaningful historical narration. And this narration is taking place in the present. As Lacan points out “history is not the past. History is the past in so far as it is historicized in the present,” it is always a present synthesis of the past (Lacan in Evans, “The Lure” 144).

This problem, the problem of meaning in history, cannot be resolved by recourse to some kind of extra-discursive “evidence” that invests the discourse of the historian with objectivity; such a possibility is undermined by the recognition of the ontological gap between the past and historical discourse. Even if traces of the past exist—in fact independently of the historian who might or might not find them—evidence, as opposed to the past and its traces, “is always the product of the historian's discourse, simply because, prior to that discourse being articulated, evidence (history) doesn't exist: only traces do” (Jenkins, Rethinking 49). Even traces that are directly accessible, like coins, written records, etc., have neither fixed meaning nor a fixed authenticity (Walsh 31). Traces are constituted as such—as objects of the historian's discourse—and acquire historical meaning through the intervention of an external cause that serves as a nodal point within the historical narrative and transforms them to historical evidence. What is implied here is that in order to produce history—that is, a meaningful narration of a succession of events—out of the meaningless series of traces of the past, a certain principle has to be introduced, a principle that serves as a point of reference, a nodal point in Laclau and Mouffe's vocabulary, around which the discourse of history is articulated. Without this framework of meaning, no “fact” can be constituted. The writing of history (historiography) presupposes some kind of transcendence (usually posited as the origin or the telos of history). It is important to note that this nodal point cannot be reduced to the succession of history itself. It can work as a cause of the historical succession only insofar as it is located outside of it—if it were reduced to a moment of this succession, it could not be differentiated from the other moments and thus its causal powers would have evaporated.

Battered Women's Refuge as Social Symbolic Space

Janice Haaken

Janice Haaken

Janice Haaken   Professor of psychology at Portland State University and a clinical psychologist in private practice. She has published extensively in the areas of psychoanalysis and feminism, gender and psychopathology, and the psychology of social movements, She is author of Pillar of Salt: Gender, Memory, and the Perils of Looking Back.

Patriarchal cultures have generated a vast folk lore narrating the quandaries of damsels in distress, overtaken by merciless villains. Such villains are a necessary storytelling convention under patriarchy, for they set in bold relief the beneficence and redemptive powers of the good male protector. For every Christ there is a Satan (or its secular equivalent), with each representing one side of the Law of the Father. The contest between these two poles of masculine authority—between protective authority and malevolent control—establish the coordinates of many a handmaiden's universe. While her naive and trusting nature may undermine her capacity to distinguish illusory and genuine guardians of her virtue, the female protagonist finds that her fate ultimately depends on her ability to discern the difference.

The battered women's movement that emerged in the 1970s intervened in this Gothic romance, displacing man the redeemer with the power of sisterhood. Shelters and crisis facilities arose, as women began to collectively name and resist male violence. Reworking psychological portraits of abused women, feminists showed how the cycle of violence was more than a series of individual repetitions of past trauma. The working through of gendered trauma required collective forms of reparation, and a politically realized vision of subjectivity. Further, the movement demonstrated that the male protectors and healers women had traditionally relied upon—the “good patriarchs” in the world of the oedipal fathers—only loosened the chains that bound her to her state of dependency. To break out of this pernicious cycle, women needed to find sanctuary or “transitional spaces” run by and for women. In psychoanalytic terms, women needed to “return” to the mother. Economic independence and legal remedies were a necessary foundation for self-development. But on the deepest emotional level, the holding, containing presence of women was essential for breaking the spell of the Gothic romance, and for creating the possibilities for genuine freedom.

The year 1970 saw the publication of Germaine Greer's famous book, The Female Eunuch. This book was without doubt an intellectual landmark within what is called the second feminist wave. The scope of both the book and the wave surpass feminist territory alone and aim at liberation as such, since they are directed against authoritarian political structures, the nuclear family, and power in general. Greer expresses this quite clearly in the last paragraph of her first chapter: “The anti-feminists have complained that the emancipation of women will imply the end of marriage, the end of morality and the end of the state…When we reap the harvest which the unwitting suffragettes sowed, we shall see that the anti-feminists were after all right.”

Meanwhile, a quarter of a century has elapsed, we are ready to reap this harvest, and indeed Greer's prophetic words turn out to be true. However, there is one snag: she herself does not seem to be very happy with the result. Quite the contrary. In an interview with The Sunday Times Magazine (March 3, 1996), she tells us that if women were in charge, the UK would return to the status of a kind of third-world country. The rest of the interview follows the same lines.

Since this reversal is rather a surprise, one is tempted to look for reassuring ad hominem explanations: she is probably frustrated, it has something to do with her age, etc. Strange as it may seem, we find an analogous, although more subtle, reversal in the work of another prominent figure of that movement, Doris Lessing. Anyone who has read her Martha Quest quatrology cannot doubt her literary talent or her left-wing feminist commitment. Nevertheless, in her recent autobiography and the ensuing interviews, she takes her distance and even goes so far as to say that she deplores its impact upon her personal life.

The crowning touch came in 1990 when Camille Paglia stormed onto the scene with her Sexual Personae, which immediately turned her into a cult figure. Indeed, her message was loud and clear: being a woman and a confirmed lesbian, she wrote a polemic plea in favour of the male cause and described femininity in a way no man had dared to do since Otto Weininger's Geschlecht und Charakter.1
